summary: In Episode 25 (Season 2) of the Muffled Minds Podcast, host Khawar Shahzad sits down with Dr. Nughza Zaheer, a Consultant Psychiatrist, to talk about why people in Pakistan are afraid of psychiatrists. They discuss why psychiatry gets softened into counselling, why a brain doctor is called a counsellor while a heart doctor is called a cardiologist, and why people hide a visit to a psychiatrist but happily share the name of their dermatologist.

Dr. Nughza explains how she chose psychiatry after her mother spent years being treated as a psychiatric patient before a tumour was finally diagnosed, and why she now rules out physical illness before diagnosing a mental one. She talks about the free clinic that starts at every wedding when relatives find out she is a psychiatrist, the myth that psychiatric medicine turns people into zombies, and why other doctors should not change a prescription a psychiatrist has written.

Much of the episode is about children: the signs parents should watch for at different ages, mindful screen time and why slow cartoons beat loud rhymes, and what schools should teach about mental health. It closes with a rapid fire round and her message to the audience: do not wait for a breakdown before getting help, and seek it from a certified psychologist or psychiatrist.

takeaways: A psychiatrist is a doctor who has specialised in psychiatry after MBBS and can prescribe medication; a psychologist is trained for therapies, and a counsellor is a broader term for anyone guiding you in something specific.
If your pancreas does not make insulin you call it diabetes, but if your brain does not make neurotransmitters you will not call it depression, yet the brain is an organ like any other.
Psychiatric medicines do not turn you into a zombie: different classes have different effects, drowsiness is a known side effect of some and is usually managed by prescribing them at night.
Give each child ten minutes of undivided attention every day, without a screen in between, so you know when something is out of the norm.
Below the age of two, screen time is not acceptable at all except for video calls to relatives; after that, keep it mindful and slow.
If you make a mistake with your child, own it and apologise, so the child learns that mistakes can be admitted and corrected.
Psychiatric medicines need time to work, so wait at least six to fourteen days for symptoms to improve, and stick to one psychiatrist who knows your history instead of doctor shopping.
You do not need to break down before getting help; seek professional help in time, from a certified psychologist or psychiatrist.
Dam and medicine are not rivals: if a spiritual practice brings peace and does not harm the patient, it can sit alongside the medicine.
